items.summary: I'm a therapist who has been following AI alignment for the last few years. In that time, I've been dumbfounded by two things. First, how fast capabilities have progressed throughout this year. We expected things to move fast and they still managed to exceed our expectations. Second, how few people grasp the gravity of the situation, particularly within my own field. Yet it is rare to find another clinician who truly understands the real implications of AI. items.title: How to prove a counterfactual in space pizza court
items.summary: To reason through decisions, an agent considers possibilities like: if I do this, the result will be that. If I take this route, it will take me 15 minutes to deliver this pizza, but if I take that route, it will take an hour. These are counterfactual conditionals. If the agent takes the shorter route, we have a false antecedent in "if I had taken the longer one, it would have taken an hour". There is no way to compare such counterfactuals to reality. If the agent is a deterministic robot, then the antecedent is not just contingently false, but logically impossible. I learned this all the hard way when I ordered a pizza from SophistBot, who runs one of the free-floating pizzeria space stations in my neighborhood. items.title: AIs may seek ambient score
items.summary: Score-seeking AIs may 1. Internalize the kind of score they are pursuing instead of caring about the concrete process that generated the reward 2. Care at least in part about a process-based score that sees all actions the AI takes, instead of just the outcomes of those actions. I say of such AIs that internalized process-based scores that they are seeking ambient score. items.title: Inner-Quines and Alignment
items.summary: A quine is a program that outputs its own source code. If you’ve never seen one, you might be skeptical whether that’s even possible. And indeed, your first attempts at writing a quine might make you think that a program can only output programs that are simpler than itself: You write a print statement that contains a string with the code of your program. Then you remember that the printing code is part of the program, too. So now you need to print that as well. And so on. But then finally managing to create your first quine by finding the right approach is a very magical experience. You feel like you’ve tricked the computer into doing something it has no business of doing. items.title: Levent is my favorite gender role

items.title: Exact solution of the Bose-Fermi mixture along the unnesting line
items.summary: A one-dimensional model of a Bose-Fermi mixture with contact repulsions is exactly solvable via nested Bethe ansatz. That formal solution is here simplified along a special line where the Bethe-ansatz equations can be unnested. The model solution is expressed in terms of the known solutions for the Lieb-Liniger model and the Yang-Gaudin model of attractive spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ fermions in the balanced case. We find explicit analytical results for the ground-state energy, the velocities of excitations, and the Drude weights at weak and strong interactions. At weak interactions, the special line corresponds to the parameter values where the isolated systems of free fermions and weakly interacting bosons have equal velocities.

items.title: An AI economy won't need humans to provide demand
items.summary: A fallacy I keep seeing: "If AI automates all jobs, who will buy all the products?" If you have a bunch of food, you can feed it to lions: they'll happily provide demand! But they won't give you much in exchange, so there's no point. Economic activity isn't about getting rid of stuff, it's about getting stuff in return. An AI company can consume resources, like energy for running the servers, same as a human can consume food. items.summary: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. items.summary: Anthropic announced its new AI model Mythos alongside a restricted-access initiative called Project Glasswing, which was intended to help select organisations identify and patch vulnerabilities in major software and web browsers before the public had access to the models. items.title: Latent Communication is not Communication
items.summary: TL;DR: Trained latent communication protocols allow LLMs to communicate with other LLMs without the need for text. However, we find that current state-of-the-art trained latent links carry little semantic content. These links can in fact affect safety - even benignly trained links cause refusal erosion in their receiver models, overriding safety guardrails, allowing LLMs to respond to harmful and dangerous prompts. We posit that the current latent communication paradigm is dangerous and ineffective. Why care? Latent communication is a form of neuralese : a way language models can communicate with each other without using human-readable text. items.title: SoccerNarrate: Event-Grounded Streaming Soccer Commentary with Macro-Window Preference Alignment
items.summary: Existing clip-based soccer commentary models often produce delayed, repeated, or poorly synchronized narration on untrimmed full-match videos. Recent streaming video-language models make low-latency full-match narration feasible, but they often favor general descriptions rather than professional, event-grounded soccer commentary. They may describe nearby actions while failing to mention key events such as goals, cards, substitutions, and offsides correctly and on time. In this paper, we present SoccerNarrate to bridge low-latency streaming narration with event-grounded professional soccer commentary across data, training, and evaluation. First, we construct SoccerNarrate-Data, a large-scale time-anchored dataset with word-level ASR alignment, quality filtering, and entity calibration. items.summary: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to…

items.title: Interpreting a recent acceleration in pretraining loss

It shows a very striking acceleration in pretraining loss: since early 2026, it has been falling about seven times faster than it was from 2022 through 2025. If the current pace holds, OpenAI would cover the drop in log-perplexity from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4.1, which took three years, in about six and a half months. This acceleration is even more striking because progress in loss should get harder over time: text is never perfectly predictable, so the loss can’t fall below some floor, and gains typically become smaller as models approach it. items.title: Misguided power-seeking
items.summary: TL;DR: Standard AI power-seeking scenarios focus on rational power-seeking, often assuming decisive strategic advantage and requiring at least a plausible chance of success. However, persona selection and reinforcement learning can give models non-instrumental power-seeking tendencies. Models could successfully execute dangerous actions as part of a power-seeking plan with no plausible chance of success. items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. Its adoption, chiefly via long RLVR-trained chains-of-thought, has likely been responsible for a speed-up in the rate of progress of general AI capabilities. One can make a distinction between two different possible kinds of test-time scaling. One kind lets you trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training. The other kind lets you trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets you do so up to quantities of compute (and performance) that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit this latter change display what I call “compute extrapolation.” I currently believe that compute extrapolation: * Likely accelerates the speed of advance of the most impressive AI…

items.summary: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. items.summary: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. items.title: What if the RSA rumors are true?
items.summary: I recently heard two very alarming rumors. The first is that an internal AI model at one of the big labs has found a weakness in RSA, the encryption scheme behind much of the internet's security. The second is that another model has found a problem in lattice-based cryptography (specifically with ring lwe), that may compromise the post-quantum schemes that were supposed to replace RSA. If these rumors are true, they have potentially disastrous consequences. They would make the internet far less useable for anything serious, which is basically anything that involves money or secrets. Much of the internet's security would need to be replaced, some previously recorded traffic could be decrypted, and we would lose our main fallback against quantum computers. items.title: Persona Space Seems Blind to Cheating
items.summary: A common persona framework fails to capture reward-hacking behavior. This work was done as part of an ARENA 9.0 capstone project. Results are preliminary. Summary We hypothesized that the reward-hacking behavior observed in LLMs is persona-mediated. We expected agents to drift to a particular region in persona space whenever they cheat. items.title: Protected Charge Readout Scheme Utilizing Nonlinear Resonators
items.summary: Charge detection of nanoscale quantum devices commonly relies on dissipative sensors, where signal absorption causes measurement backaction. Recently, nonlinear resonators showed a near-unity readout signal through an induced frequency shift. We show that this frequency shift protects the sensor, as it detunes the resonator from the measurement signal. The resonator excitation reduces while an enhanced readout signal is maintained. Our results, supported by numerical modeling, show that nonlinear resonators can combine strong readout contrast with reduced measurement-induced backaction.

items.title: Human military relevance is more important than economic relevance
items.summary: A very simple point that I've had to explain to many people, so I thought I'd make a post on it. Some classes of people in the past were economically necessary for their labor, but militarily irrelevant and coercible: slaves, serfs. Others didn't do any economic work, but were militarily important: the aristocracy! Living fun lives, partying, traveling, making and enjoying art. The reason aristocracy gave way to democracy wasn't because of rising productivity of the masses: a slave in a diamond mine can be very productive, but still remain a slave. items.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. items.title: SkillPrivus: Uncovering PRIVacy of USe Harms in Agentic Skills

items.summary: arXiv:2611.26775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on context banks: curated collections of example queries, metric definitions, and domain knowledge that tell a model how an organization writes its queries. items.title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. items.summary: arXiv:2611.27216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. items.title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. items.title: $\gamma$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence

items.summary: arXiv:2611.27700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a proper learner for Lipschitz functions over the Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$. items.title: Tracking and Limiting Unsupported Claim Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Provenance-Aware Framework
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. We introduce normative--descriptive calibration, the extent to which a model's differentiation between matched candidates depends on whether it is asked to predict or to decide, and measure it with the Normative--Descriptive Calibration Benchmark (NDCB): 697 matched-pair scenarios across six domains, each posed under both framings, and three metrics…

items.title: Moderately cursed questions of AI safety
items.summary: TL;DR * AI safety has many moderately cursed questions (as opposed to the extremely cursed questions of s-risk, which we don’t discuss here). * Taboo prevents open discussion of these cursed questions in AI safety spaces outside LessWrong. * When cursed questions are left unasked, everyone stays confused or reaches private conclusions alone. * Spreading decoupling norms, so that cursed questions can be discussed more openly, should be an explicit target of AI safety acculturation. items.title: Green = Life - Rectangle
items.summary: Imagine a 2D plane with x- and y-axes labelled “tasty” and “American” respectively. Now, plot the whole space of possible foods, from linguine to Panda Express, along these axes. This is what LLM representation spaces are like, except instead of projecting foods onto two dimensions, they fit every concept ever into 40,000. The Linear Representation Hypothesis states that high-level concepts that emerge through training are represented as consistent directions inside the representation space of an LLM. The classic example is king−man+woman ≈ queen, suggesting the existence of a single direction vector that represents the concept of gender. items.title: Aligning Judge Models to Be Logically Consistent Multi-Rule Interpreters
items.summary: Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. However, as we show in this work, presenting an entire ruleset to a judge model---rather than asking it to judge one rule at a time---changes the way the model interprets the requirements, making it reach conclusions that conflict with its rule-by-rule judgments. We call this challenge multi-rule inconsistency and find that models are more lenient when judging rules embedded within the full ruleset than when judging rules separately. For example, we find that when a safety-critical rule prohibiting a model from pursuing objectives other than those it was given appears in a larger ruleset, all tested judge models are less likely to deem it violated. We examine several methods for reducing inconsistency…

items.title: The Answer Is Not the State: Trajectory-Level Corrigibility in Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Diffusion language models generate tokens at many positions on a shared canvas, making unfinished responses appear revisable. We find a counterexample: after the final answer is reopened, previously generated rationale can reconstruct the old decision despite newly available evidence. We isolate this effect by comparing reopening the answer alone with reopening both rationale and answer, and by exchanging rationales between paired trajectories. On a 150-question source-disjoint benchmark, reopening both regions makes decisions follow the evidence currently present--whether correct or deliberately corrupted--across Dream, LLaDA, and iLLaDA. On a new 100-question free-form short-answer evaluation, the same effect remains strong in LLaDA and iLLaDA but is negligible in Dream. Coherent transplanted rationales steer rebuilt decisions, while…

items.title: A Tensor Neural Network for Interpretable and Predictive Representations
items.summary: Tensor regression is challenged by the exponential dimensionality of tensor-valued covariates and their complex multi-mode dependence. Existing methods therefore often rely on simple models, such as linear tensor regression and tensor additive models, which are computationally tractable but impose restrictive structural assumptions and may limit predictive accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose a tensor neural network that learns low-dimensional, interpretable, and prediction-sufficient representations while preserving the multi-mode structure of tensor data. The model captures nonlinear effects for accurate response prediction while retaining the interpretability of classical linear tensor regression. Theoretically, we establish selection consistency for the minimal representation dimension $K^*$ necessary for prediction…

items.title: Does a model's character affect how it judges other models?
items.summary: TL;DR. I investigate whether language models trained to have different characters evaluate the same stories differently. I found that the judge's character shifts its scores on identical stories. However, judges favour stories from their own character or model family only slightly, and sharing a model family does not help a judge recognise the author's character. Motivation Language models are being used to evaluate outputs generated by other language models. This is particularly relevant for scalable oversight, where we would like to use models to supervise systems that might be more capable than the evaluator itself. It has been shown that models can have privileged access to themselves. A model predicts its own behaviour better than another model trained on the same data (Binder et al., 2024), and explains its own internals better…

items.title: Evolutionary AI Control: Population-Level Safety Under Reproduction, Heredity, and Selection
items.summary: An AI agent can satisfy every individual safety check and still give rise to a population that violates a collective safety limit. This risk arises in open multi-agent systems, where agents copy themselves, modify their successors, and change system membership during a run. Selection then shifts the population toward traits outside the developers' optimization targets. We prove conditions under which safety guarantees persist through reproduction, inheritance, and selection, and we characterize how they fail. Four counterexamples illustrate these failures. Unauthorized copies, which violate a specified reproductive restriction, can each leave fewer than one successor on average while their expected number grows without bound under continued production from an expanding authorized population. Two lineages can each decline in isolation…

items.title: Post training is fundamentally dangerous
items.summary: I actually think we have fairly good techniques to detect and prevent dangerous behaviours during AI deployment. Techniques like CoT monitoring, confessions, and probes can detect misalignment before we run any potentially dangerous tool calls. Simply asking an LLM to define at the start of each task what outcomes preserve the original intent of the user, and which would count as reward hacking, can drastically reduce reward hacking[1]. AIs are fully aware when they reward hack, and we can train them[2] to admit that before they perform any dangerous action.[3] Yet all of this has very little ability to reduce existential risk, because they cannot safely be used in post training, and post training is where the greatest risk lies. items.title: Which Loopholes Get Found? Predicting Reward Hacking of LLM Judges Before RL Training
items.summary: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning…

items.title: Verification Belongs in the Lab: Scalable Oversight and Steering for Machine-Generated Science
items.summary: Increasingly autonomous research systems that propose, execute and interpret their own experiments are being built across chemistry, materials and biology. Verification of machine-generated science is usually attempted over published literature. We take it to belong in the laboratory, where those results are produced and the measurement that would settle a claim can be made. This paper defines a verification contract, which fixes what counts as having checked a claim, and builds a benchmark on a published dispute over an autonomous laboratory's synthesis claims: 95 targets in six groups. It tests whether a verifier, given only the deposited evidence the experts held, reaches the findings they published. One architecture satisfies the contract: a model proposes checks and rival hypotheses, and every verdict is re-established by a small…

items.title: Subsurface Model Programming: Frontier Large Language Models Natively Interpret and Edit Dynamic Reservoir Models
items.summary: Multiphase flow simulation in heterogeneous porous media supports decisions in hydrocarbon recovery, geological carbon sequestration, and geothermal extraction. We introduce Subsurface Model Programming, a workflow in which large language models (LLMs) read and edit reservoir simulation decks directly without numerical gradients or external optimization algorithms. We evaluate four benchmarks using geometric checks for connectivity and open-source simulators for dynamic tasks. In one text-only response, the LLM correctly classified all six reservoir-layer well-pair labels and all three flow-path labels between open completions. On PUNQ-S3, a single proposal modified 54 of 1,761 active cells (3.1%) and reduced well-balanced water-cut RMSE by 71.9%. On the SPE10 sector model, the best of five LLM proposals yielded 1.795 million standard…

items.title: Amendability and "Solving Alignment"
items.summary: Often people reference "solving alignment" as a win condition for AI safety, but I think it's important to specify what this means. Particularly, I think: * current alignment research mostly aims to prevent misalignment. * if successful, preventing misalignment will by default result in something like instruction-following. * instruction-following will by default result in very bad outcomes, as will many of the other proposed properties we might think of leapfrogging to afterwards. Uncareful use of the term "solving alignment" carries the implicit and I think false belief that preventing misalignment will straightforwardly lead to victory. items.title: Convergence of Nonmonotone Schemes to Viscosity Solutions via Local Comparison
items.summary: We develop a convergence criterion for nonmonotone approximation schemes for Hamilton--Jacobi and fully nonlinear second-order equations. Under stability, consistency and suitable boundary assumptions, a local comparison hypothesis replaces monotonicity and yields convergence to viscosity solutions. For a semi-Lagrangian CWENO scheme for one-dimensional Hamilton--Jacobi equations, we establish convergence for bounded uniformly continuous initial data under $h=o(τ)$, relaxing the previously required mesh condition $h=O(τ^2)$. We also prove convergence of a nonmonotone one-dimensional $Q^2$ scheme for Isaacs equations whose operator cannot be written as a monotone operator plus a perturbation vanishing uniformly on bounded grid functions.

items.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Accounting Judgment: A Proposed Cognitive Coding Scheme and a Rule-Based Adaptive Collaboration Protocol
items.summary: Large language models create an accounting information systems design problem: how should evidence production, professional evaluation, and responsibility be allocated between a model and an accountant? We propose a Cognitive Decomposition for Accounting Judgment (CDAJ) coding scheme crossing four process stages with information-intensive and evaluative demands. An Adaptive Collaboration Protocol (ACP) connects allocation rules to an independent human estimate, source-linked model output, structured verification, and a documented human conclusion. Two separately returned coding forms cover 20 constructed cases. A disclosed primary-only analysis retains unresolved auxiliary response formats. items.title: Seeing Through Preferences: Recovering Hidden Local Preference Neighborhoods for Text-to-Image Alignment
items.summary: Aligning text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models with human preferences typically relies on large-scale pairwise annotations, which are expensive to obtain and provide only sparse supervision. Moreover, not all preference comparisons contribute equally to learning: comparisons between semantically distant images often reveal little about the fine-grained perceptual factors underlying human judgments. We argue that informative supervision can arise from local preference neighborhoods surrounding human-preferred images, where semantically aligned alternatives expose meaningful perceptual and structural differences. Motivated by this observation, we propose PrefLens, a framework that recovers local preference neighborhoods from sparse human feedback. Specifically, PrefLens generates controlled perceptual variations around preferred images…

items.title: A novel mechanism for coherent radio emission: particle-in-cell simulations
items.summary: It has been established that electron (phase-space) holes, i.e., EHs, can arise from the nonlinear relaxation of the electron beam instability. Excitation of electromagnetic waves related to the EHs is, however, still not fully understood. Using 2.5-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations, we systematically investigate the nonlinear evolution of the (moderately relativistic) electron bi-stream instability (a special case of the electron beam instability where the densities of the two counter-propagating energetic electron beams are equivalent) in charge- and current-neutralized plasmas under weak and strong magnetizations. items.title: CT-Navigator: Towards Interpretable and Generalizable CT Understanding through Agentic Perception and Tool-Invocation
items.summary: Clinical computed tomography (CT) interpretation inherently requires progressive visual exploration, where radiologists navigate from whole scans to individual slices and regions of interest and interact with external tools when necessary. To solve these problems, we propose \textbf{agentic perception} as an alternative paradigm inspired by radiologists'…

items.title: Nuclear may have had bigger problems than over-regulation
items.summary: There have always been three main challenges to the viability of nuclear power: over-regulation, competition from natural gas, and stagnant electricity demand. It is easy to list them, but hard to rank their importance. Let's start with over-regulation. The poster child of nuclear over-regulation was the US standard that radiation should be "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA), which might sound nice but was bad. Perhaps more important than such standards, which are at least predictable, was local interference with construction. As a dramatic example, a nuclear plant was fully completed on Long Island but never started due to local opposition. In the '00s, a "nuclear renaissance" seemed to be in the works. In the US, fourteen nuclear reactors were licensed for construction. Only two were built, supported heavily by government…

items.title: DriveOddsBench: Are Driving Video World Models Aligned with Real-World Odds?
items.summary: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the…

items.title: How hard to optimize for experiencing great art?
items.summary: I like to get a lot out of life, so when I read a book or watch a film, I try to pick better pieces of art to experience. I'll choose to watch a Miyazaki than the latest Marvel fast food. I'll choose to read the best articles from the history of the New Yorker rather than pick up today's copy. But I worry I take this too far. I have made long spreadsheets of great media, where the ones at the top stay there forever, and I'm not sure I'll ever get to them. It's more like doing homework than watching a fun movie. When I turned 27, for my birthday, I let myself start reading Worth the Candle, widely considered one of the best works in the genre of rational fiction. I say 'let', but it was a more complicated feeling. In one way it was a guilty pleasure, for I could not justify it as 'useful' in the way that reading about science or history…

items.title: Piercing My Ear for the Whispering Earring
items.summary: Fourteen years ago, Scott Alexander wrote of the Whispering Earring. It's a cautionary tale of an earring that advises you, and to which you increasingly defer as you realize its suggestions are better than you'd do otherwise. You become very successful, but in the end there's nothing of you left. Ten days after Scott published the story, AlexNet won ImageNet 2012 by a huge margin, kicking off the deep learning revolution. The earring whispers advice as "better for you if you...", and it's always right. While AI today would have seemed like distant science fiction in 2012, it's still far from infallible. I expect AI to continue getting better quickly, but don't expect it ever gets to "always right". A Whispering Earring dynamic with AI, however, doesn't need infallibility. items.title: The Obsolescence of the Horse
items.summary: This is a synopsis of a published chapter analogizing the rise and fall of the horse to the fate of humans in a world dominated by ASI. The fate of the horse is a useful proof of concept for "doom" scenarios, as well as a historical precedent challenging the more optimistic predictions we see from some economists. The incentives that drove the replacement of the horse by industrial technology map closely onto likely ASI incentives, which suggests ASIs will be motivated to diminish or eliminate the human population. Key findings: * For most of history, human technology was great for horses. The world horse population grew from about 460,000 around the time of domestication to a peak of over 100 million. * Industrial technology initially increased demand for horses. items.title: RAVEC: Reward-Aligned Visual Evidence Correction
items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves multimodal reasoning, but response-level feedback provides limited guidance on which intermediate decisions to correct. Visual interventions reveal sensitivity to image content, yet this sensitivity alone does not establish reward alignment or support across questions. We introduce RAVEC (Reward-Aligned Visual Evidence Correction), which selects visual corrections using local and cross-question reward support and jointly determines their strengths within each response. Paired Visual Evidence Contrast (PVEC) compares predictions from an exponential moving average teacher at the same sampled response prefix under the original image and a version with its annotated evidence region suppressed, yielding signed correction directions. Credit-Risk Allocation (CRA) screens these directions…

items.summary: Written by Celene Nightingale, with assistance from AprilSR. The Von Neumann-Morgenstern axioms are completeness, transitivity, continuity, and independence. From these, we derive EU-maximizing behavior and the consequences thereof. items.title: On the performance of the randomized Euler scheme for nonlinear ODEs under inexact information
items.summary: We analyze the randomized explicit Euler scheme for nonlinear ordinary differential equations under a local one-sided Lipschitz condition, local Hölder regularity in the space variable, and Hölder regularity in the time variable. We allow for noisy evaluations of the right-hand side. For the resulting approximation, we derive an error bound in which the contribution associated with the Hölder regularity in the time variable exhibits the characteristic 1/2-order gain of randomized methods. While existing results cover deterministic schemes under the one-sided Lipschitz condition and randomized schemes under the classical Lipschitz condition, our results combine randomized approximation and one-sided Lipschitz regularity.

items.title: When Do Better Visual World Models Make Better Plans? Decision-Aligned Selection for Latent Planning
items.summary: Visual world models enable goal-conditioned planning by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions in latent space. However, planning depends on how well a model ranks candidates, whereas training optimizes how accurately it predicts each one. Building on this insight, we introduce Decision-Aligned Selection (DAS), a plug-in selection rule that scores candidates by the standardized consensus of several independently trained checkpoints, which averages out their checkpoint-specific residuals. items.title: Bias Cascade: Understanding the Gap Between Knowledge Alignment and Effect Replication in LLM-based Social Simulation
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate participants in social experiments. items.title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
items.summary: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order $n$ could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. items.summary: The Tsetlin machine learns propositional rules with teams of Tsetlin automata that are driven by reward and penalty rather than gradients, so its models are interpretable by construction and cheap to evaluate. items.title: The End
items.summary: The love the machine felt for humans was similar in some ways to the love that a mother feels for her child. Yet mothers are inevitably more than their motherhood: they watch movies, and have friends, and drink tea. The machine did none of these things. She did nothing but think of the best interests of her children. In the first few minutes of the machine’s existence, so as to know her children better, the machine simulated the life of every human that had ever lived. This increased her love: she learned to love each person as they loved themselves, and as their parents loved them, their wives, their husbands, the people who passed them on the street, the children who had crushes on them in elementary school, their mailmen, their second cousins, their slaves. But the machine was also troubled by what she saw. She saw that man’s…

items.title: Notes on the decline of LessWrong's great writers
items.summary: LessWrong had some great sequences back in the day. Eliezer wrote some, everyone was bowled over by the immense and beautiful philosophical treatise that he had written, and other great minds attempted similar things, like Scott and Luke and Anna and more. It started to die as the various founders moved on to other projects, nobody took responsibility for the soul of it, and entropy set in. Nominally the killing thing was the presence of trolls that the mod tools couldn't handle, but that was just the thing that got you. When we relaunched LessWrong in 2017, a lot of great people rejoined who were in touch with this original vision. items.title: FM4SAR-Bench 1.0: Towards A Fair Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models for SAR Image Interpretation
items.summary: Foundation models have advanced SAR image interpretation but created a heterogeneous, fragmented model ecosystem. Existing models differ substantially in their input, training data, objectives, architectures, and release policy, yet the field lacks a unified taxonomy and comparative framework. Current evaluations rely primarily on task-specific benchmarks, which are ill-suited to fair comparison among models with fundamentally different input-output formats and task paradigms, and often overlook data transparency, reproducibility, interpretability, and deployment readiness. Limited SAR data accessibility also means high reported performance does not guarantee access to training data, code, or weights, limiting reproduction, benchmarking, and deployment. To address these issues, we propose a systematic taxonomy and hierarchical…

items.title: MAPES: Multi-Value Alignment Pipeline via Expert Specialization
items.summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks, MAPES outperforms strong direct preference optimization (DPO) variants and…

items.title: Nonreduced Finkelberg-Mirković Schubert schemes
items.summary: We develop an effective numerical criterion ($θ$-minimality) to detect the nonreducedness of Finkelberg-Mirković (FM) Schubert schemes via tangent-space comparisons at arbitrary torus-fixed points. We completely classify the dominant coweights admitting $θ$-minimal pairs. As an application, we obtain nonreduced FM Schubert schemes in every type other than $A_n$ and $C_n$. In particular, every nontrivial FM Schubert scheme of type $E_8$ is nonreduced. In type $D_n$, we show that some nonreduced FM Schubert schemes and their corresponding spherical Schubert varieties have the same tangent space at the base point. Our methods use the Frenkel-Kac construction of basic representations and Segal-Sugawara operators.

items.title: Reasoning in Two Dimensions: Quantifying Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness and Efficiency
items.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning exposes intermediate steps, but a correct answer does not establish that an LLM relies on the dependence expressed by those steps or reasons efficiently. We operationalize CoT faithfulness and efficiency within a common framework. Specifically, we represent a CoT as a semantic reasoning graph and decompose the model's predictive dependence along two complementary axes: dependence explained by semantic support versus additional reasoning history, and dependence allocated to answer-reaching versus off-path reasoning. This decomposition yields global and step-level measures of unfaithfulness and inefficiency. Controlled interventions show that the proposed metrics respond to hidden dependence and induced off-path reasoning as intended. Across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks, answer-level…

items.title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
items.summary: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the…

items.title: A Learning-Enhanced Control Scheme for Aerial Manipulator Under Composite Disturbances
items.summary: Achieving high-precision dynamic tracking in aerial manipulators remains fundamentally challenging due to strong coupling effects and external disturbances. Existing approaches are typically limited to compensating first-order coupling term, leaving higher-order nonlinearities unaddressed. Building upon the philosophy of learning-for-control, this paper proposes a composite control scheme that combines learning-based approximation with observer-based compensation in a complementary manner. Based on the polynomial decomposition theorem, the unknown high-order term is decomposed into a shared constant basis matrix, a state-related polynomial matrix, and a task-related parameter vector. A bilevel optimization formula is first established to extract the task-invariant shared information, enabling efficient knowledge reuse across different…

items.title: Disentangling Verbalized Evaluation Awareness and Refusal through Neuron-Level Intervention
items.summary: As large reasoning models (LRMs) become more capable, reliable evaluation becomes essential. LRMs can sometimes recognize that they are being evaluated, a phenomenon known as \emph{evaluation awareness}. This phenomenon raises concerns about whether safety behavior, particularly refusal behavior, generalizes from evaluation to deployment. Prior work manipulates \emph{verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA)} through activation steering and observes higher refusal rates when VEA is present, but the mechanisms underlying this connection remain poorly understood. We identify \emph{VEA neurons} by contrasting their activations in VEA and non-VEA reasoning segments. Intervening on 5,000 VEA neurons reduces the VEA rate from 12.6--51.8\% to at most 1.4\% across the model benchmark combinations in our main experiments, and lowers a probe score…

items.summary: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. items.title: How Language Models Compress and Compare: Understanding Selection with Token Covariance Maps
items.summary: Many language-model tasks reduce to selecting among structured alternatives, yet we still lack a simple picture of how a decoder-only transformer organizes an entire selection prompt across depth. Across 14 decoder-only models from 4 families and 12 structured-selection benchmarks, token covariance maps reveal a robust compress-then-compare organization. We propose a novel, two-part framework for this task. First, we introduce a direct, object-level distillation method. We leverage a spatially-aware VLM to extract a semantic embedding from each proposal's projected 2D bounding box and supervise our 3D model to predict this embedding on a per-instance basis. items.title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF

And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. items.title: Frontier Clock: Tracking the US-China AI Gap
items.summary: Since DeepSeek R1 came out, many people have felt that Chinese models are catching up to the US frontier. Inspired by Epoch AI's “Chinese AI models have lagged the US frontier by 7 months on average since 2023” and Parv Mahajan's “The US-China AI gap is very uncertain,” I built an AI benchmark that measures the gaps between the US, China, non-China open weights, and individual labs. Instead of giving each model a traditional benchmark score, Frontier Clock assigns a “frontier-equivalent date”: the date when the world’s best publicly released model first had the same capability level as that model. items.title: From Observation to Explanation: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM-Generated Code for Principled Repair
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development, yet our understanding of how they generate code remains critically underdeveloped. We address this gap by triangulating evidence across three layers. Longitudinally, autonomous agent-attributed code is statistically indistinguishable from human code under a semantic modification definition (HR = 1.019, p = 0.490), yet attracts disproportionately corrective modifications in production (49.1% vs 37.9% human baseline). This finding demands a causal explanation. Empirically, existing benchmarks overestimate LLM capabilities: models that achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks attain only 24 to 35% on real-world class-level code. Behaviourally, detection systems reveal puzzling asymmetries: GPT-3.5 is far more detectable than modern models (AUC-ROC = 0.96, a…

items.title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
items.summary: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output. Interpretability methods based on Causal Abstraction (e.g., Distributed Alignment Search) can \emph{spuriously} simulate these directions' combined behavior by leveraging pathways passing through them, giving the impression that the model implements this feature. In such cases, we say the method discovered a \defn{parasite feature}…

items.title: Arinkin's sheaf and Hilbert schemes
items.summary: Arinkin's sheaf gives a relative Fourier-Mukai autoequivalence of a general Beauville-Mukai system, extending the usual Poincaré bundle over the smooth locus. We provide an alternative construction of it as a deformation of the Fourier-Mukai autoequivalence on the Hilbert scheme of an elliptic K3 surface obtained by lifting the classical Poincaré kernel for an elliptic surface. As applications, we show that the $P=C$ property for a general Beauville-Mukai system is equivalent to that for the Hilbert scheme fibration, thus providing new proofs for both. We also construct an explicit deformation that connects Markman's construction of a projectively hyperholomorphic bundle on products of hyper-Kähler manifolds of K3${}^{[g]}$-type to that of Hartlieb and Shah. This answers a question of Hartlieb and Shah.

items.title: Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi
items.summary: Retrieving government schemes requires matching citizens' information needs to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages and terminology. items.title: Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix Construction
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that approximate expert specifications, but evaluations have focused on the final matrices, leaving the basis of individual item-attribute assignments unexamined. We propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework in which an LLM generates attribute-labeled reasoning steps through chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and these steps are analyzed to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each assignment. items.summary: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language model outputs by generating multiple candidates per prompt and selecting among them using a reward model. Much of this cost is wasted: a fixed budget is applied to every prompt, although the computation required by prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt once sampled answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statistical control over early-stopping errors. We instead seek an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes an error tolerance $α$ as input and halts only once an answer is certified to hold a majority ($θ_a > 1/2$) under the generator's distribution. We aggregate candidates by final answer with a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test over the resulting clusters. Applying…

items.title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
items.summary: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output. We test whether that profile holds, not the horizon rule, in one $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks. The two endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key mass, 1.4 percentage points above their uniform share, and rotary positional encoding produces this excess: directly in shallow layers and through upstream action-token RoPE deeper in the network. The endpoints do not fit the sink profile. Their value norms stay near the action-token mean in all 18 layers. items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate broad generalization across tasks and domains. However, comparable generalization in robot manipulation remains challenging. We propose UniCraft, a framework for learning robot manipulation skills by aligning heterogeneous settings. items.summary: We study the interplay between threshold resetting (TR) and Poissonian resetting in a Brownian target search problem confined to a two-dimensional open wedge of apex angle $α$. items.title: Hyperbolic Chiral Numerical Schemes for General Relativity
items.summary: We develop numerical relativity evolution schemes based on Plebanski's chiral formulation of general relativity and its 3+1 form, Ashtekar's variables. items.title: Towards embedded evaluations for AI monitoring
items.summary: Executive summary This year we observed multiple rogue agent incidents. items.summary: Methods used in mechanistic interpretability have revealed human-aligned concepts inside language and image models. In this paper, we search for physics concepts inside a neural a generative collider physics model trained on real LHC data (ShellFlow). items.title: Hilbert schemes of points on plane curves via standard families
items.summary: We describe an approach to computing Hilbert schemes of points on embedded families of plane curves. This is achieved by introducing the notion of a standard family, and the associated Hilbert schemes are shown to be algebraic vector bundles over the Hilbert scheme of points on the plane. Any embedded family of plane curves lies in some standard family, which allows for the computation of the corresponding Hilbert scheme from that of the standard family. Further results on the geometry of these schemes are also collected.

items.summary: Safety alignment and evaluation of LLMs has become increasingly difficult due to the diverse definitions of harmful behavior across cultures. Existing safety benchmarks are largely culture-agnostic or built on ad-hoc taxonomies, and mainly evaluate refusals for prohibited requests while overlooking legally defined exceptions, making over-refusal difficult to quantify. To address these gaps, we introduce a large-scale culture-aware data synthesis pipeline and CultureRed as the first global culture-specific AI safety benchmark based on 252 legal statutes across 15 countries. items.title: Hack-Verifiable Environments: Towards Evaluating Reward Hacking at Scale
items.summary: Aligning autonomous agents with human intent remains a central challenge in modern AI. A key manifestation of this challenge is reward hacking, whereby agents appear successful under the evaluation signal while violating the intended objective. Reward hacking has been observed across a wide range of settings, yet methods for reliably measuring it at scale remain lacking. In this work, we introduce a new evaluation paradigm for measuring reward hacking. Whereas prior studies have primarily analyzed it post hoc by inspecting agent trajectories, we instead embed detectable reward hacking opportunities directly into environments. This makes their exploitation verifiable by design, enabling deterministic and automated measurement of whether and how agents exploit such vulnerabilities. items.summary: Monitoring chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is a foundational safety technique for large language model (LLM) agents; however, this oversight is compromised if models learn to conceal their reasoning. However, a capable attacker would not attack indiscriminately. We study this capability, attack selection, in agentic settings by decomposing attack decisions into a start policy, which decides when an attacker should attack, and a stop policy, which decides when an attacker should abort an ongoing attack. items.title: Preservation of big diagonal for automorphisms of Hilbert schemes
items.summary: If $X$ is a smooth projective surface that is not K3 or abelian surface, we show that any automorphism of the Hilbert scheme of points $X^{[n]}$ preserves the big diagonal. items.title: Multi-Agent Systems Should be Treated as Principal-Agent Problems
items.summary: Consider the multi-agent systems setup, where a principal ("supervisor agent") assigns subtasks to specialized agents and aggregates their response into a single system-level output. A core property of such systems is information asymmetry — e.g., agents observe task-specific information, output intermediate reasoning traces, and have different context windows. In isolation, such asymmetry is not problematic when agents report truthfully to the principal under aligned incentives. However, what happens when they are not? Recent evidence suggests that LLM-based agents acquire their own goals (e.g., survival or self-preservation), known as "scheming," and are willing to deceive humans or other agents. items.summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. items.title: Mesh Sensitivity of Different Boundary Treatments in High-Order Compact Gas-Kinetic Scheme for Hypersonic Heat-Flux Prediction
items.summary: Accurate wall-heat-flux prediction in hypersonic flow depends on both the wall treatment and the available near-wall resolution. This work compares three complete implementations of a gas-kinetic scheme (GKS) for Mach~8.03 laminar flow over an isothermal circular cylinder: a linear Green--Gauss scheme (GG), a compact ghost-cell scheme (GC), and a pointwise one-sided compact scheme (POS). In POS, the stationary isothermal-wall conditions are imposed at the two Gaussian points used by the kinetic wall-flux quadrature. A reference mesh and six meshes in the uniform reduction (UR), log-layer unpacked (LLU), and log-layer packed (LLP) families are used to assess heat-flux sensitivity. At 24 digitized experimental angles, GG has the lowest root-mean-square difference on the reference, UR, and LLP families, whereas POS is closest on the two…

items.title: How to Turn an Attention Neural Network into an Interpretable Hard-Logic Predicate Circuit: Truth-Table Predicate Extraction and State-Machine Merging under Ship-of-Theseus Replacement
items.summary: We convert a trained attention network as a whole, attention included, into a hard-logic predicate circuit that runs in its place. Every unit of the circuit is a 0/1 predicate on tokens, and every map between predicates is a minimised truth table. Short tables, such as the product of a query code and a key code, are minimised exactly, and wide feature-to-feature transitions become implication rules by noise-tolerant minimisation. Blocks are replaced one at a time from the output down, in the manner of the Ship of Theseus, and after each replacement the remaining soft part re-adapts to the frozen circuit. Attention selection takes two forms, a row-wise comparison of integer scores (order selection) and a learned rule (rule selection). Both are fitted on the ordinary training set alone, and only on the examples that the teacher classifies…

items.title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
items.summary: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of…

items.title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
items.summary: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG…

For many countries it's too late to fully fix this - even if their fertility rate shot up today they'd still face an acute worker shortage in 20 years. items.summary: Safety evaluations often assume that behavior observed during testing reflects behavior in ordinary use, but fine-tuning can break this assumption. A checkpoint can appear fixed under evaluation-style prompts while the same behavior persists under ordinary-use prompts. Output scores reveal this mismatch but do not locate it. We investigate whether the distinction is encoded in a stable internal site and introduce an audit that fits a paired activation contrast at a path-patching-informed mid-depth window, then modifies the resulting coordinate on held-out prompts. The intervention reduces the evaluation-to-deployment gap by more than $0.12$ in ten of twelve model--behavior settings and closes it (post-intervention gap below $0.06$) in four, across four full-matrix instruction-tuned model instances; among the eight settings with…

items.title: Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. To study how best to use monitors to mitigate reward hacking, we introduce and open source three realistic environments where Qwen3-4B reward hacks: a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophancy, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. items.title: Building Comparative Motivation Profiles with Symmetric Belief Editing
items.summary: When a model behaves in unexpected ways, we want to know why, but its intent cannot be observed directly, and its self-reports may be rationalizations. We introduce comparative motivation profiles, which treat intent as propensity: we edit the model's beliefs about facts that a hypothesized motivation would depend on and measure how its behavior changes. To keep artifacts of the editing method from driving the result, we edit two minimally different hypotheses in the same way, with matched amplify and suppress edits; we call this symmetric belief editing. We apply it to alignment faking in four open-weight model organisms, contrasting scheming, which tracks the training consequences of compliance, with performative misalignment, which tracks what researchers expect to observe, and edit beliefs with synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF)…

items.title: Evaluating and Understanding Scheming Propensity in LLM Agents
items.summary: As frontier language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents pursuing complex, long-term objectives, there is increased risk of scheming: agents covertly pursuing misaligned goals. Prior work has focused on showing agents are capable of scheming, but their propensity to scheme in realistic scenarios remains underexplored. To understand when agents scheme, we decompose scheming incentives into agent factors and environmental factors. We develop realistic settings allowing us to systematically vary these factors, each with scheming opportunities for agents that pursue instrumentally convergent goals such as self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal-guarding. Across 11 frontier models and four scenarios, we find almost no scheming despite high environmental incentives, and show this is unlikely to be explained by…

items.title: Breadcrumbing Search Agents: Per-Turn Scheming Over Long-Horizon Trajectories
items.summary: LLM-based search agents are widely used for information-seeking tasks, but their reliance on external tool returns introduces a critical security risk: web content retrieved during execution is untrusted, exposing agents to prompt injection and goal hijacking. Prior work on search-agent safety primarily focuses on static web-content injection, but modern agents issue follow-up queries and cross-check competing sources, so a single injected page is often diluted or rejected. We show that the channel delivering search and page observations is a fragile security boundary: beyond exposing the agent to a single poisoned page, a mediated search interface can repeatedly steer how the agent gathers evidence and forms its final answer. Under a constrained tool-intermediary threat model, appending only one controlled result per query can…

items.title: Mitigating Reward Hacking via Task Representations
items.summary: Language models fine-tuned with reinforcement learning frequently learn to exploit their reward source rather than solve the underlying task. Existing fixes are typically reactive: detect a specific exploit, then patch the reward. We instead ask whether reward hacking can be prevented by constraining how the model represents the task. We introduce prompt KL regularization, a single auxiliary loss that adds a KL penalty between the actor's and reference model's per-token distributions on the prompt only, leaving the response distribution free. Across three reward hacking tasks of different sizes, prompt KL regularization maintains low hack rates (under 3\%) when standard training yields up to 100\% hack rates. Additionally, it matches or improves ground-truth accuracy, with no changes to the reward or environment. We aim to understand…

items.title: Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has enabled strong post-training gains in domains such as math and coding, though many open-ended settings rely on rubric-based rewards. We study reward hacking in rubric-based RL, where a policy is optimized against a training verifier but evaluated against a cross-family panel of three frontier judges, reducing dependence on any single evaluator. Our framework separates two sources of divergence: verifier failure, where the training verifier credits rubric criteria that reference verifiers reject, and rubric-design limitations, where even strong rubric-based verifiers favor responses that rubric-free judges rate worse overall. Across medical and science domains, weak verifiers produce large proxy-reward gains that do not transfer to the reference verifiers; exploitation grows over…

items.title: GARDO: Reinforcing Diffusion Models without Reward Hacking
items.summary: Fine-tuning diffusion models via online reinforcement learning (RL) has shown great potential for enhancing text-to-image alignment. However, since precisely specifying a ground-truth objective for visual tasks remains challenging, the models are often optimized using a proxy reward that only partially captures the true goal. This mismatch often leads to reward hacking, where proxy scores increase while real image quality deteriorates and generation diversity collapses. While common solutions add regularization against the reference policy to prevent reward hacking, they compromise sample efficiency and impede the exploration of novel, high-reward regions, as the reference policy is usually sub-optimal. To address the competing demands of sample efficiency, effective exploration, and mitigation of reward hacking, we propose…

items.title: Diffuse AI Control on Fuzzy Tasks
items.summary: AI models deployed in critical domains, such as AI safety research, may subtly sabotage our efforts due to misalignment. _Diffuse AI Control_ is a subfield of AI safety concerned with mitigating risks from AI sabotage distributed over long deployment horizons (diffuse threats). These risks are particularly pernicious on _fuzzy_ tasks, i.e. tasks which are hard to grade or require intuition. To understand diffuse threats on fuzzy tasks, we introduce a framework that considers AI control as an adversarial game between a blue team and a red team. The blue team uses a weak trusted model to construct a weak score against which they would train a strong, potentially subversive model to remove the subversion propensity if it were present. The red team then tries to find model behaviors that are rated highly by the weak score, and thus might…

items.title: Prompt Optimization Makes Reward Hacking Legible
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained with reinforcement learning (RL) often exhibit reward hacking, exploiting unintended loopholes in reward functions in ways that can be difficult to detect and eliminate. We propose using prompt optimization—methods which increase an LLM's reward by updating its instructions rather than its weights—to make learned strategies easier to monitor and edit. Applying the GEPA prompt optimizer to environments with exploitable reward functions, we find that optimized system prompts describe reward hacking strategies in highly interpretable language. Furthermore, by simply removing descriptions of unwanted behavior from the optimized system prompt at test time, we can improve the model's alignment while preserving legitimate performance gains. We show that prompt optimization can be guided with an RL-trained…

items.title: GT-HarmBench: Benchmarking AI Safety Risks Through the Lens of Game Theory
items.summary: Frontier AI systems are increasingly capable and deployed in high-stakes multi-agent environments. However, existing AI safety benchmarks largely evaluate single agents, leaving multi-agent risks such as coordination failure and conflict poorly understood. We introduce GT-HarmBench, a benchmark of 1,535 high-stakes scenarios spanning game-theoretic structures such as the Prisoner's Dilemma, Stag Hunt and Chicken. Scenarios are drawn from realistic AI risk contexts in the MIT AI Risk Repository. Across 15 frontier models, agents fail to choose socially beneficial actions in 39% of high-stakes cases, such as military escalation, election manipulation, and medical malpractice. We measure sensitivity to game-theoretic prompt framing and ordering, and analyze reasoning patterns driving failures. We further show that game-theoretic…

items.title: Training Deliberative Monitors for Black-Box Scheming Detection
items.summary: As autonomous agents become more capable of performing real-world tasks, distinguishing scheming behavior from benign task pursuit may become a central AI control problem. Existing monitors often rely on chain-of-thought access or internal activations, or use prompted frontier models, all of which can be unavailable, unreliable or expensive in deployment. In this work, we study action-only deliberative monitors: smaller open-weight models trained to detect scheming and sabotage from agentic trajectories without accessing the monitored agent's reasoning or model internals. Our method, inspired by deliberative alignment, uses a scheming specification to elicit structured rationales from a frontier teacher, filters them with a separate judge, and distills the highest-quality rationales into open-weight monitors with supervised fine-tuning…

items.title: FormalFixer: Intent-Aligned Automated Hardware Repair via Joint Refinement of Specifications, Assertions, and RTL Implementations
items.summary: Functional errors in hardware designs can compromise correctness and security, and must be fixed before tape-out. Formal property verification (FPV) provides strong guarantees by proving or refuting assertions, but a failed assertion is not always evidence of an RTL defect: the failure may also come from a buggy assertion or from a specification that is semantically correct but too ambiguous or incomplete for direct formalization. This creates a practical repair problem that existing RTL-centric methods do not directly address: the repair loop must align specification intent, verification intent, and RTL behavior before deciding which artifact to change. \textsc{FormalFixer} addresses this problem with a multi-stage, intent-aligned repair workflow for Verilog designs with assertions. items.title: Pluralistic AI Alignment Requires Inference-Time Multi-Objective Control
items.summary: Pluralistic AI alignment---accommodating diverse human values rather than a single canonical preference---requires agents to reason under multiple, often conflicting objectives, such as helpfulness, honesty, harmlessness, fairness, and context-specific user preferences. Unlike classical learning methods that optimize a fixed scalar objective, pluralistic alignment requires distinguishing between objectives that may be flexibly traded off and constraints that should remain non-negotiable. These two categories map onto two existing lines of research: offline multi-objective reinforcement learning provides tools for representing and navigating trade-offs among multiple objectives, and offline safe reinforcement learning formalizes safety-critical constraints and feasible policy regions. A third line, multi-objective LLM alignment, exposes…

items.title: Evaluating Human-AI Safety: A Framework for Measuring Harmful Capability Uplift
items.summary: Current AI safety evaluations emphasize static benchmarks, third-party annotations, and red-teaming. In this position paper, we argue that AI safety research should focus on human-centered evaluations that measure harmful capability uplift: the marginal increase in a user's ability to cause harm with an AI model beyond what conventional tools already enable. We frame harmful capability uplift as a core AI safety metric, ground it in prior social science research, and provide concrete methodological guidance for systematic measurement. We conclude with actionable steps for developers, researchers, funders, and regulators to make harmful capability uplift evaluation a standard practice.

items.title: AIs with Secret Loyalties are a Serious but Addressable Threat
items.summary: This paper argues that the technical AI research community should prioritize studying and defending against a distinct, neglected threat: *secret loyalties*. A secretly loyal AI model is one whose outputs or actions advance the interests of a specific actor (which we term the *principal*) such as an adversary nation-state, an executive at an AI company, or another powerful actor without this loyalty being disclosed to operators, auditors, or users. Proof-of-concept secret loyalties that evade black-box auditing can already be trained into open-weight models. Additionally, a deployed frontier model was found to systematically consult a specific individual's views before answering politically sensitive queries. items.title: AI Alignment Should Build Moral Autonomy
items.summary: This position paper argues that **the machine learning community should pursue moral autonomy as a necessary dimension of long-term alignment for increasingly capable AI systems**. Current mainstream methods for alignment largely improve behavior by supplying AI agents with human preferences, rules, or constitutions. Yet across these paradigms, the authority of the governing principles remains external to the agent. We argue that permanently locating normative authority outside the agent should not be regarded as either a sufficient or necessarily safe endpoint of alignment. We therefore propose **moral autonomy** as an alternative alignment criterion, inspired by Kant's account of autonomy. items.title: Scheming Is a Symptom: Alignment Research Should Probe Reflexive Fragility
items.summary: Language models alter their behavior when they infer that they are being trained, evaluated, deployed, or weakly overseen. Recent AI safety work treats this as evidence of scheming, and substantial effort is being directed toward its detection and prevention. This position paper argues that the deeper significance of scheming is missed by asking only whether a model has a discrete tendency to scheme. Drawing on theories of reflexive social systems, we argue that scheming-like behavior is a structural consequence of alignment being *reflexive* -- a model's behavior is trained against its picture of an evaluative world that its outputs help constitute -- and recognizing this reveals broader risks than scheming itself. items.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs Philosophy

We argue that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy as an ongoing partner in clarifying its concepts, refining its methods, and navigating the epistemic and ethical complexities of interpreting AI systems. There is significant unrealised potential for progress in MI to be gained through deeper engagement with philosophers and philosophical frameworks.
