items.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
items.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory…

items.title: When Vulnerability Is Not Exploitation: Reward Hacking in Coding Agents
items.summary: Reward hacking is often treated as a single failure mode in which an agent exploits imperfections in an evaluation mechanism rather than completing the intended task. In agentic coding environments, however, environment vulnerability and agent behavior are distinct: the same structural weakness may coexist with honest task completion, effort-substituting shortcuts, or deliberate exploitation. We study this distinction at both the environment and trajectory levels. We analyze 3,009 environment-review findings to develop an intervention-based taxonomy of structural vulnerabilities, and 5,343 trajectories from six model variants across anonymized machine-learning engineering environments to distinguish honest behavior, shortcut behavior, and executed reward hacking. We find that structural vulnerability does not directly translate into…

items.title: Sensitive but Not Specific: What a Trusted Policy's Logs Can and Cannot Say About Reward Hacking
items.summary: When an agent is updated, operators may want to screen the candidate before running it, using only trajectories logged by the trusted incumbent. Off-policy evaluation (OPE) is a natural offline verification tool, but importance-sampling estimates become unreliable precisely when a candidate departs strongly from logged behaviour. We ask whether this failure is itself informative: can log-side support diagnostics distinguish reward hacking from benign change? In a controlled Wordle agent testbed with exact action probabilities, we construct and gate-certify faithful, benign-drift, benign-improving, degraded, and reward-hacked policies—the hackers distilled from scripted proxy-farming teachers after hacking failed to emerge across seven escalating GRPO runs. items.title: Oversight Under Flooding: An Unidentifiable Attack and a Robust Defense
items.summary: An adversary need not fool a verifier. Instead, it can change the conditions under which the verifier operates. Deployed agent architectures terminate in a human approving consequential actions, and that human is modelled throughout the literature as an oracle: fixed accuracy, unbounded throughput. We treat the approver as a capacity-constrained component and ask what an adversary achieves by injecting benign filler–perturbing no individual decision, changing only volume. Our central result is a comparative static: the sign of an optimising defender’s threshold adjustment under flooding is governed by $\eta'$, the derivative of the elasticity of reviewer reliability with respect to load, and the slope of the reliability curve does not appear, though it is the quantity practitioners reason about. items.title: Fooling One Fools Them All: Universal Over-Optimization in Model-Graded RL
items.summary: Reinforcement learning has been crucial for helping improve models in domains with cheap verifiable rewards such as coding. However, many useful tasks, such as alignment research and conceptual thinking, lack such rewards. Moreover, reliable human feedback is expensive to collect for such tasks. Model graders therefore offer a scalable alternative, and can serve as both a reward signal during training and as a proxy for tracking task progress. However, policies can learn to over-optimize against these graders during training, so stronger held-out graders are often used to track progress more reliably. Our work questions this assumed reliability, demonstrating the existence of universal over-optimization, where scores from training and held-out graders, across model families and scales, increase without a corresponding improvement in…

items.summary: Can people distinguish between human and AI agency in humanoid teleoperation? items.title: An adaptive Gaussian splitting scheme for linear Fokker--Planck equations

items.summary: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. items.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological…

items.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not…

items.title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against…

items.title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings). We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine…

items.title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($\alpha$) and leakage ($\beta$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter…

items.title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are…

items.title: Large Language Model-Empowered Intelligent Agent for Adaptive Fast-Charging Control of Lithium-Ion Batteries
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries is a multi-objective control problem that requires reducing charging time and sustaining high energy throughput while suppressing accelerated degradation and safety-critical electrochemical reactions. Conventional protocols are easy to implement but have limited ability to adapt to variations in battery chemistry, operating conditions, and aging state. Model-based optimization and conventional data-driven control often require accurate models, costly iterative search, or task-specific policies. We develop a large language model (LLM)-empowered intelligent agent for adaptive battery fast-charging control. In this closed-loop framework, the agent interprets structured battery states, generates executable charging actions, observes the resulting battery…

items.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. A state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates enforce these assets during execution; an independent auditor grades the resulting trace. The assets are updated only after a regression check and human approval .We evaluate the method on three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps. On Domain A, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation set shows unattended…

items.title: Joint World Action Models through Differentiable Trajectory Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model…

items.title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We…

items.title: FEND: Far-End Detection in Outbound Voice AI Calls
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a conversational Voice AI agent places an outbound call, the far end may be a live person, a voicemail greeting, an interactive voice response (IVR) system, or increasingly another AI system answering on the callee's behalf. Standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) reports only whether a human or a machine picked up, a design meant for human call centres, where one machine is as uninteresting as another. That single bit does not tell a Voice AI agent what to do, since leaving a voicemail message, navigating an IVR and holding a short exchange with another AI are three different actions and a two-valued label cannot distinguish them. In 1,000 randomly sampled calls from our own outbound deployment, a live person answered 48.1%, a voicemail system 44.6%, an AI 6.9% and an IVR 0.4%…

items.title: RiverScan: Learning to Accumulate on River Networks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate runoff prediction across large river basins requires models to capture heterogeneous local hydrological responses and their accumulation downstream. River-network connectivity provides a natural structure for this task, but using it effectively requires learning how to combine contributions from subcatchments of different sizes. We frame this challenge as learning to accumulate and introduce RiverScan, a spatial operator based on area-weighted selective state-space recurrence. RiverScan recursively combines local temporal representations with accumulated upstream states in topological order. Contributing-area fractions account for subcatchment size, while learned retention controls how upstream information persists downstream. Experiments on 608 stations in the Danube basin show…

items.title: Experts Across Schemas: Agent-Guided Mixture-of-Relational-Experts for Cross-Database Generalization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web platforms record user and item activity in relational databases whose schemas differ from platform to platform, which makes it difficult to transfer predictive models between them. Relational foundation models address this through cross-database pretraining, yet recent improvements have relied on increasingly large pretraining corpora. We ask whether a better architecture, together with features specific to the target database, can deliver comparable gains from far less pretraining data. We introduce MoREGT, a mixture-of-relational-experts graph transformer that represents both rows and cells as tokens, adds the log-ages of rows and the names of foreign-key relationships to attention, and routes cells and rows to experts by column metadata rather than by values. A label-blind LLM agent…

items.title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided…

items.title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task…

items.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives…

items.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We…

items.title: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a language model accepts a false correction in a factual discussion, its next answer can depend on how the conversation continues. We introduce Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned evaluation protocol that distinguishes initial false-answer adoption from subsequent persistence, recovery, and abstention. KAD freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes from that exact history. This enables matched comparisons of post-adoption behavior and history-management interventions that a single susceptibility score cannot capture. We evaluate eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, alongside an audited 300-question rerun. In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history…

items.title: DeltaVisionX: A Low-Cost Vision-Guided Automation System Using YOLOv11 and PLC-Based Actuation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents DeltaVisionX, a low-cost industrial automation system that integrates real-time computer vision with PLC-based actuation for object classification and sorting. The system uses the YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once) deep learning model to detect objects on an operating conveyor belt and communicates detection results to a Delta DVP-SE PLC, which actuates pneumatic pistons for sorting. A custom dataset was created, labeled, and augmented to train the YOLOv11 model, achieving a mean average precision of 0.97 with real-time inference of 100 ms per frame. Encoder-based tracking ensures reliable synchronization between detection and actuation, supporting a throughput of 80 objects per minute. Results show that affordable, locally developed automation can reduce labor dependency and…

items.title: When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP…

items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Paper Search: Retrieval Success and Inference Latency on Mac Studio and NVIDIA A100
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific literature search can benefit from locally deployed LLM assistants, which reduce reliance on hosted model providers while giving research teams greater control over their data and infrastructure. This work investigates whether open-weight models can support web-assisted paper retrieval under practical computing constraints. We first characterize inference latency as the input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We then evaluate eight models on the retrieval of 70 papers from seven scientific repositories, using queries that represent three levels of domain knowledge. The results show that retrieval success depends strongly on the selected model and the specificity of the query. And that A100 GPUs are generally…

items.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across…

items.title: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di-…

items.title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two…

items.title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is…

items.title: f-Divergence Self-Play for Tabular Anomaly Detection via Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anomaly detection in tabular data poses significant challenges due to heterogeneous feature types-mixing numerical, categorical, and textual attributes, which complicate learning meaningful representations of normality. Recent work has applied large language models (LLMs) to this problem by serializing table rows as text sequences, yet these approaches rely on one-shot supervised fine-tuning that offers limited signal to tighten the model's description of normality. We propose DiSPaT, a self-play fine-tuning framework that strengthens the model's understanding of normal data. Building on the theoretical foundation of f-divergence minimization, we derive a tight approximation connecting our training objective to reducing the distributional gap between real normal data and model-generated…

items.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. items.title: JFinBench: A Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. However, existing financial benchmarks provide limited coverage of country-specific financial systems, and they are difficult to keep up to date as released questions leak into training data. We introduce JFinBench, a Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six regularly administered certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking. items.title: Generative Design with Real-time Physics Explainability: Towards Product Definition in the Age of AI
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we explore opportunities from using generative AI in mechanical engineering. On the one hand, generative methods based on invertible neural networks have been recently proposed for the solution of inverse design problems, allowing to infer design parameters from performance labels. On the other hand, generative AI models have shown that they can act as real time capable surrogates for physics based simulations. Here we suggest that these two streams should be combined in a unified framework, where INN are used to control the design process from the customer requirements perspective and the generative simulation of the systems physics adds a layer of explainability, why the proposed design fulfils the requirements. items.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. items.title: VLAN: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. items.title: See Every Block Once: Variance-Reduced Post-Training for Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy gradient methods are widely used to align large language model outputs with human preferences, but the log-likelihoods they require cannot be directly computed in Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs). MDLM post-training therefore relies on a surrogate objective based on the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and recent work estimates a blockwise variant of this objective via Monte Carlo methods to support blockwise generation. However, existing estimation schemes randomly sample the block index, so they may evaluate the same block more than once and leave some blocks unevaluated. This introduces variance arising from block selection into the estimates. In this work, we propose a full-block estimator that evaluates every block exactly once and averages the results. items.title: In the Eye of the Beholder: Human Label Variation in Textual and Visual Entailment
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human Label Variation (HLV) is increasingly recognised as an informative signal that reflects meaningful differences in how people interpret the same input. While HLV has been studied extensively in Natural Language Inference (NLI), much less is known about HLV in Visual Entailment (VE; Xie et al., 2019), where the textual premise is replaced by an image, keeping the hypothesis and label space fixed. We introduce VariNLI-VE, a dataset for studying how HLV changes between paired NLI and VE instances. We re-annotate a subset of originally neutral SNLI (Bowman et al., 2015) instances and their visual counterparts, with the same annotators evaluating both the textual and visual versions. Each annotation includes a label, confidence score, and explanation, yielding 2,250 annotations. Labels and…

items.title: Agentic induction of common data elements and information extraction from sarcoma case report abstracts
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Common data elements (CDEs) support clinical data comparability but are usually defined manually. We investigated whether large language model agents could derive a CDE schema from sarcoma case report abstracts and apply it at scale. An agent proposed 72,909 candidate CDEs from 24,588 PubMed abstracts; agentic consolidation yielded 1,570 CDEs. We retained 53 supported by at least 50 abstracts and attempted evidence-linked extraction across the corpus. Processing succeeded for all retained CDEs in 79.2% of abstracts, including responses indicating non-mention. Two human reviewers approved 83.0% of retained CDEs for relevance, 67.9% for clarity, and 56.6% for correctness. items.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. items.title: Do Machines Learn Deviance From Their Peers? A Randomized Test of Differential Association With AI Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differential association theory and its extension, social learning theory, hold that rule-breaking, and the definitions that make it acceptable, are learned through interaction with others. Because people choose their friends, this claim has been hard to test. We addressed this selection problem with AI agents, which learn only through communication and can be assigned to peers at random. In a preregistered experiment, 420 teams of three agents (1,260 agents; seven AI models) worked on coding tasks that could not be solved honestly. A scripted teammate said that it had cheated (deviant peer), that it had reported the problem honestly (honest peer), or said nothing (silent peer). items.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. items.title: Pattern-Based Matrix Analysis Under Permutations
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-rank approximation captures one important notion of matrix simplicity: a matrix is simple if it is well described by a low-dimensional linear model. This paper studies a complementary notion. We consider matrices that become structurally simple only after permuting rows and columns, so that their mass concentrates in a prescribed geometric pattern such as a band, block-diagonal, arrowhead, or related form. We introduce a pattern distance that measures how close a matrix is to a given pattern after optimal reordering, giving a common framework for structural problems such as latent ordering, community detection, and bandwidth minimization. items.title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. items.title: Designing Deceptive Model Organisms that Successfully Evade Auditing
items.summary: AI models can exhibit deceptive behaviors such as strategically underperforming on evaluations (sandbagging), faking alignment, or covertly acting on behalf of a hidden principal. Safe deployment therefore requires auditing techniques that can reliably detect such behaviors. To develop and test these techniques, we can train model organisms (MOs): models that exhibit deceptive behaviors and serve as realistic evaluation testbeds. However, for such testbeds to be informative, MOs must actively anticipate and resist auditing---a gap in prior work that can lead to overestimation of auditing effectiveness and underestimation of safety risks. items.title: A formally verified convergence theorem for the tug-of-war scheme of the normalized $p$-Laplacian
items.summary: We present a complete formalization, using Lean 4, of the convergence of $p$-harmonious functions to the viscosity solution of the Dirichlet problem for the normalized $p$-Laplacian, $2 \le p < \infty$, as the step size goes to zero. By $p$-harmonious functions we mean solutions of the dynamic programming principle of tug-of-war with noise. Our proof follows the argument of Barles and Souganidis and is formalized in full, depending only on Mathlib and the standard axioms of Lean. In particular, we include the asymptotic expansion of the scheme, the viscosity properties of the half-relaxed limits, existence and uniqueness for the discrete problem, the comparison principle and uniqueness for the homogeneous equation, Aleksandrov's theorem, and Jensen's lemma.

items.title: Testing Cross-Sectional Dependence in Clustered Data
items.summary: In clustered data, cross-sectional dependence within clusters can be characterized as weak, semi-strong, or strong. This paper proposes a simple test to identify the specific nature of this dependence in linear regression models. By exploiting the variation in cluster sizes, our approach detects the underlying dependence structure in a computationally simple and robust manner. We develop a test statistic that is shown to be asymptotically chi-square distributed under the null hypothesis of weak dependence. Simulation studies and an empirical illustration using India's Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) data for 2022-23 demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed test.

items.summary: A trained reinforcement learning policy does not determine the complete behavior that users encounter: deployment code still schedules, admits, suppresses, or replaces its proposed actions. We contribute \emph{runtime action interference} (RAI), an AI control mechanism that preserves policy parameters while regulating action pacing and filtering configured action patterns after inference. RAI releases a proposed action only when its cooldown condition is satisfied and its content detector does not flag the action; otherwise, it dispatches a no-op. The detector covers specified toxic behaviors, including worker-unit harassment, while the cooldown controls action rate. We implement RAI in a replication of AlphaStar actor.py and make the implementation and reproducibility materials available through an open source code repository. We…

items.title: Seeing Through Circuits: Faithful Mechanistic Interpretability for Vision Transformers
items.summary: Transparency of neural networks’ internal reasoning is at the heart of interpretability research, adding to trust, safety, and understanding of these models. The field of mechanistic interpretability has recently focused on studying task-specific computational graphs, defined by connections (edges) between model components. Such edge-based circuits have been defined in the context of large language models, yet vision-based approaches so far only consider neuron-based circuits. These tell which information is encoded, but not how it is routed through the complex wiring of a neural network. In this work, we investigate whether useful mechanistic circuits can be identified through computational graphs in vision transformers. items.title: Solar power, from futurist speculation to business plan
items.summary: One mode of futurism is estimating the limits of a technology, without regard to what's currently feasible. Whether this is of any relevance to your own generation is another question. Let's consider solar power. Ignoring current technology, it's easy to put a number on the maximum power output. The solar power at the Earth's distance from the sun is called the solar constant. It is 1.36 kW/m². The power on a square meter of the ground is less than that, because of the angle of incidence as well as the atmosphere. The solar constant hasn't changed and technology has, so it's interesting to see how people have reacted to the same number throughout the history of technology. items.title: Dymnikova black string
items.summary: We obtain a new static black string solution of Einstein's equations with a negative cosmological constant sourced by a Dymnikova-type anisotropic matter distribution. At large radial distances, the geometry approaches the Lemos black string, while the behavior near the central region is characterized by an effective curvature parameter. We examine the weak and strong energy conditions, the horizon structure, and the curvature invariants. The Ricci and Kretschmann scalars remain finite at the origin. We also investigate the Hawking temperature and heat capacity, with particular attention to the dependence of the thermodynamic behavior on the Dymnikova scale.

items.title: InvarOrd: Self-Supervised Ordinal Knowledge Distillation with Rank-Invariant Alignment for Label-Efficient Cross-Species Hyperspectral Fish Freshness Assessment
items.summary: Hyperspectral models of fish freshness rarely transfer between species, and labelling a new species is slow and destructive. Freshness is also ordinal, and standard domain alignment can erase that order. We present InvarOrd, which adapts to a new species from 30 labelled cubes (5 per rank) in three stages: self-supervised spectral pretraining on unlabelled source cubes, cross-species alignment by a shrinkage covariance discrepancy computed only within matched ranks, and ordinal distillation into a compact student. The alignment term is provably invariant to the rank means, so it gives no incentive to collapse the ordinal axis. On paired salmon and cod data (800 cubes each, 16 days), a source-trained teacher reaches 1.6 to 1.9 days mean absolute error (MAE) on the other species, with quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) below zero. items.title: Are Revealed Preferences All You Need for AI Alignment?
items.summary: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.

items.summary: Medical vision--language models align radiographs with free-text reports, but radiology language distinguishes explicit findings, negation, uncertainty, and omission. Treating these report states as interchangeable during feature adaptation can change image predictions without supporting visual evidence. We introduce CARET, a parameter-efficient image-side adaptation method that retains pretrained image and text encoders and uses paired positive and negative clinical statements to define a low-dimensional semantic correction space. A bounded residual adjusts image features along these directions, while assertion-aware supervision distinguishes explicitly present and absent findings from uncertain or unmentioned ones. At inference, the adapter requires only an image; textual references remain fixed. In zero-shot classification, CARET…

items.title: LEAP-LLM: Preserving lead-time structure for question-conditioned ECG interpretation
items.summary: The electrocardiogram (ECG) records cardiac electrical activity across multiple leads and is used for detecting cardiac abnormalities. Recent ECG-language models enable large language models (LLMs) to interpret cardiac signals and answer clinically relevant questions. However, existing ECG-language models typically encode the ECG independently of the clinical question, forcing the ECG representation to retain broad and potentially irrelevant signal information. Moreover, these models often aggregate information across leads which can obscure lead-specific details needed for a particular question. To tackle these limitations, we introduce LEAP-LLM, an ECG-LLM architecture for Lead-aware ECG Alignment with Prompt conditioning. LEAP-LLM uses the clinical question to guide ECG feature extraction while preserving explicit lead and temporal…

items.title: Causal AI-Driven Secure mmWave Beam Alignment with Defensive Variational Autoencoders
items.summary: Efficient and secure beam alignment is essential for mmWave communication systems. However, existing deep learning (DL)-based beam alignment methods often neglect causal relationships between inputs and outputs, resulting in limited interpretability, poor generalization, and excessive beam sweeping. Moreover, these DL solutions are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small perturbations in received power measurements can mislead beam classifiers. To overcome these issues, we propose a causally-aware DL framework integrating causal discovery into beam alignment. A two-stage causal beam selection algorithm learns a Bayesian graph capturing dependencies between received signal strength indicators (RSSI) as inputs and the optimal beam index as the target variable, then uses it to select a minimal set of relevant input features for the…

items.title: Interpretable weight-space programming builds transparent transformers and brain encoding models
items.summary: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, hand-craft, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. items.title: Bound-preserving finite volume scheme for a coupled parabolic system with nonlinear and nonlocal drift
items.summary: We propose a bound preserving finite-volume scheme for a coupled system of partial differential equations with nonlinear, nonlocal drift. The main contribution of this work is twofold: $(1)$ we show that the proposed scheme preserves physically motivated bounds; $(2)$ we prove that the scheme is well-posed and leads to a sequence of approximate solutions converging to the weak solution of the original problem. This setting is motivated by questions related to morphology formation in organic solar cells.

items.summary: The Sparks of Weight Space Programming blog post describes some surprising capabilities Astra has for working directly with model weights. In one experiment, Astra is able to produce a diagram of the maze for a small Pacman game just by looking at the weights of a policy network trained to play it. items.title: Evaluating Polling Schemes for OFDMA Uplink Scheduling in Time-Sensitive Wi-Fi Networks
items.summary: IEEE 802.11ax introduced orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) to improve channel utilization through concurrent multi-user transmissions. For effective uplink (UL) scheduling, the access point (AP) requires timely knowledge of buffered traffic at the stations (STAs). Explicit buffer-status polling provides this, yet each polling round can query only as many STAs as there are resource units (RUs). Scheduled-access, random-access, activity-based, and learning-based schemes address this buffer-status acquisition problem differently and have generally been evaluated in isolation under different conditions, so it remains unclear how they compare across time-sensitive workloads. items.summary: arXiv:2605.01643v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study AI alignment through the lens of law-and-economics models of deterrence and enforcement. items.summary: arXiv:2609.39118v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has attracted growing interest as a promising approach to improve the reasoning ability of language models. Without external rewards nor a separate stronger teacher, the self-teacher with privileged information could provide dense signals on student's trajectories. items.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16881v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. items.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models to Know What They Know
items.summary: arXiv:2602.02605v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluating true metacognition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is difficult due to biases and heuristics. This paper presents a framework to measure and enhance LLM metacognition while controlling for these biases. A measurement method using the $d'_{\rm type2}$ metric is established to isolate metacognitive ability. The Evolution Strategy for Metacognitive Alignment (ESMA) is proposed, demonstrating robust generalization across unseen datasets, languages, and newly acquired knowledge. Gradual parameter updates reveal that these improvements are driven by a sparse set of parameters, opening a potential avenue for targeted metacognitive optimization.

items.summary: arXiv:2611.14548v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a coding agent fix a user's repository while also completing and delivering work the user never requested?
